questionText: Which statement keeps task exposure, substitution potential and employment effect apart?

answerOptions.text: A high exposure value proves the same share of jobs will go
Exposure and substitution potential describe tasks or technical possibilities; they do not directly predict adoption or net employment
Once one core task can be automated, the whole occupation counts as abolished
The three terms name the same statistical quantity

explanation: The OECD Employment Outlook 2023 describes employment in occupations at high risk of automation across the OECD countries studied. The IAB substitution potential describes the share of core tasks that would be technically automatable. Neither is an adoption rate. Neither is a forecast of job losses.

questionText: How do you get a defensible comparison for an AI-assisted task?

answerOptions.text: Take one time estimate without a comparison task or quality check
Test the same bounded task with and without assistance, and record time, errors, quality and human rework
Generalise from one good demo to every occupation
Measure productivity by the volume of text produced

explanation: Same task, defined quality criteria, documented rework. Only then do you see whether assistance saves time, merely shifts errors or creates extra review in your workflow.

questionText: Which description fits practical AI literacy best?

answerOptions.text: Programming, training models, analysing data
Speaking English, using international AI tools, collecting certifications
Understand the system's purpose and limits, review the output, and mind data protection, responsibility and escalation
Spotting deepfakes, programming chatbots, maintaining databases

explanation: Practical AI literacy joins system understanding to review and confident action. Article 4 of the AI Regulation requires providers and deployers to take measures fostering a sufficient level of literacy among their staff and other people they deploy. An identical level of training for every single person it does not guarantee.

answerOptions.text: The right to program AI systems yourself
On the introduction or use of technical equipment intended to monitor employees' behaviour or performance
The right to train employees on AI tools
The right to reject every AI system outright

explanation: Section 87(1)(6) BetrVG covers the introduction and use of technical equipment meant to monitor behaviour or performance, where no statutory or collective-agreement rule exists. The right sits with the works council. If the two sides do not agree, Section 87(2) lets the conciliation committee decide.

questionText: When is image, audio or video content a deepfake under Article 3(60) of the AI Regulation?

answerOptions.text: Through elaborate manual editing by specialist graphic designers
When it is AI-generated or manipulated, resembles something existing and would falsely appear authentic or truthful to a person
Only through state intelligence services with specialist hardware
By simply copying and blending existing material

explanation: Article 3(60) needs three things at once: AI generation or manipulation, resemblance to existing people, objects, places, entities or events, and a false impression of authenticity or truth. A particular technique or amount of reference material it does not prescribe.

questionText: Which statement about when Article 50 of the AI Regulation starts to apply is correct?

answerOptions.text: From 2 February 2025
From 2 August 2026
From 1 January 2027
This duty has not been adopted yet

explanation: Article 50 has applied since 2 August 2026. Providers of covered generative systems mark in machine-readable form under paragraph 2; deployers generally disclose deepfakes visibly under paragraph 4. For systems on the market before 2 August 2026, Article 50(2) applies from 2 December 2026 under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

questionText: What do you do first with a suspected deepfake?

answerOptions.text: Call the Federal Criminal Police Office at once and file a complaint
Forward the content to everyone you know so they can check it
Do not share it publicly; preserve source location, time and available evidence locally
Publish your own fact-check on social media

explanation: Every public pass-along can grow the reach. Preserve the original source, check provenance and context, and only then take the right platform, authority or private route.

questionText: Which statement about Section 22 KUG is correct?

answerOptions.text: The right to publish works of art without a licence
The right to delete images made by AI
As a general rule, portraits may be distributed or publicly shown only with consent; Section 23 holds statutory exceptions
Protection for journalists doing undercover research

explanation: Section 22 KUG holds the consent rule for distributing and publicly displaying portraits. Section 23 holds the exceptions and, in paragraph 2, a balancing of interests. Your voice, Section 22 KUG does not protect on its own.

questionText: Which account of the COMPAS controversy is supported?

answerOptions.text: The system worked flawlessly and fairly for every group
ProPublica reported different error rates; Northpointe pointed to similar calibration within the risk bands
The system was technically defective and produced random results
The system was used only in Florida and had no further effects

explanation: For the Broward County scores it examined, ProPublica reported differences in error rates. Northpointe disagreed and held calibration against that. Where base rates differ, the two fairness criteria generally cannot be met at once.

questionText: What did Gender Shades find for commercial gender classification?

answerOptions.text: Every system recognised faces with an error rate below 5 percent
Error rates differed only slightly between the four groups studied
Only older systems showed bias; modern ones are free of it
The highest error rate for lighter-skinned men was 0.8 percent, and for darker-skinned women it reached 34.7 percent depending on the system

explanation: Gender Shades tested binary gender classification, not identifying people through facial recognition. What it measured was substantial intersectional performance differences. A training-data cause for each vendor it did not prove.

questionText: Which statement about Article 22 GDPR is correct?

answerOptions.text: The right to have all your data deleted
Article 22 concerns solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effect, and it holds exceptions and case-dependent safeguards
The right to inspect the AI system's source code
The right to switch the model off

explanation: Article 22(1) covers solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effect. Paragraph 2 holds exceptions. Where a contract requires it or the person explicitly consented, paragraph 3 requires at least human intervention, a chance to express a point of view and to contest.

questionText: Which statement about deepfake detectors is correct?

answerOptions.text: Modern tools spot every deepfake with almost 100 percent accuracy
A result depends on model, data and threshold; neither a positive nor a negative result is proof on its own
Only public authorities have access to reliable detection tools
Reverse image search reliably spots every AI-generated image

explanation: A detector works under its own training and test conditions. Compression, crop, post-processing, unknown generators and the threshold change what its result is worth. Provenance and context you cannot skip.

questionText: Which tool splits videos into keyframes, triggers reverse searches and shows available metadata?

answerOptions.text: Any AI text detector
InVID/WeVerify (weverify.eu)
Google Lens
TinEye (tineye.com)

explanation: InVID/WeVerify (weverify.eu) is a research tool for verifying images and videos. It generates keyframes, supports reverse searches and shows available metadata. A verdict on truth it does not deliver.

questionText: Which statement about historical training data is precise?

answerOptions.text: Because AI developers deliberately build discriminatory systems
Because training data are always too small, whatever their composition
Because there is no way to build fair AI systems
Historical data can hold unequal structures; the model effect also depends on target, features, evaluation and deployment

explanation: Data can mirror earlier selection or power structures. Whether that turns into a harmful effect is decided at the same time by sample, labels, target, modelling, thresholds, testing and deployment.

questionText: Which statement about the EU AI Act and deepfakes is correct?

answerOptions.text: The EU AI Act bans all deepfakes with immediate effect
The EU AI Act has no rule on AI-generated content
Article 50 separates technical provider marking from visible deployer disclosure; the competent complaint route has to be checked against current information
Deepfakes matter only to providers, not to individuals

explanation: Article 50 does not ban deepfakes across the board. Providers of covered generative systems generally mark output in machine-readable form, deployers generally disclose deepfakes visibly. Exceptions and transition rules stay to be checked. Article 85 provides for complaints to the competent market surveillance authority; under the KI-MIG that is generally the Bundesnetzagentur, unless a sector authority is competent.
